lessons.title: Preacher, Prosecutor, Politician, or Scientist?
lessons.key_idea: We often defend, attack, or seek approval for our views, but thinking like a scientist means treating beliefs as hypotheses to test.

lessons.title: Confident Humility: The Sweet Spot
lessons.key_idea: The best thinkers pair belief in their ability to learn with humility about whether they currently have the right answer.

lessons.title: Finding Joy in Being Wrong
lessons.key_idea: Detaching your identity from your opinions lets you enjoy discovering mistakes, because each one means you've learned something.

lessons.title: Fight About Ideas, Not People
lessons.key_idea: Disagreement about tasks and ideas makes groups smarter, as long as it doesn't turn into personal conflict.

lessons.title: Debate Like a Dance, Not a War
lessons.key_idea: Skilled persuaders find common ground, use a few strong arguments, and ask questions instead of overwhelming people with force.

lessons.title: Open Minds by Listening First
lessons.key_idea: Motivational interviewing shows that curious questions and genuine listening help people find their own reasons to change.

lessons.title: Build a Life of Rethinking
lessons.key_idea: Creating psychological safety at work and regularly rechecking our own plans keeps rethinking a habit, not a crisis.

plan.title: Think Again
plan.author: Adam Grant
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's structure, core arguments and main examples well, though I would avoid quoting specific passages or exact figures from memory.
plan.one_liner: The smartest move isn't knowing more. It's being willing to unlearn what you're sure of.
plan.summary: Organizational psychologist Adam Grant argues that in a fast-changing world, the ability to rethink and unlearn matters more than raw intelligence. Most of us slip into three mental modes. We preach to defend our beliefs, prosecute to prove others wrong, and politick to win approval. Grant urges us to think like scientists instead, treating our opinions as hypotheses to test. He explores confident humility, the surprising joy of discovering we were wrong, and why healthy disagreement about ideas makes teams smarter. He then turns outward, showing how to open other minds through curious questions and genuine listening rather than force. Finally, he looks at building schools and workplaces where rethinking is safe, and at revisiting our own life plans before they become traps.
